paper_title: Belief-Trajectory Energy: Measuring the Path to a Prediction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) progressively revise their predictions across Transformer layers, yet we typically observe only the final output, discarding the trajectory through which it is formed. We introduce Belief-Trajectory Energy(BTE), a model-grounded measure that characterizes an input through the layerwise predictive revisions it induces in a model. By mapping intermediate states into a shared predictive space, BTE provides a principled measure of belief change that can be summarized as either a scalar or a structured depth profile. Theoretically, we show that local BTE corresponds to predictive revision under the Fisher-Rao geometry, while the sequence of revisions captures information beyond the initial-to-final belief change. Empirically, scalar BTE provides a model-relative signal of difficulty across diverse reasoning tasks, while richer BTE representations support human-LLM review detection and fine-grained generator attribution, reaching up to $0.998$ macro-AUROC and $95.6\%$ eight-way attribution accuracy. Further analysis shows that BTE develops throughout pretraining and is selectively reshaped by targeted training, demonstrating that the resulting measurement reflects what the scoring model has learned. Together, our results establish belief trajectories as a principled model-grounded signal and suggest a broader perspective in which learned models can themselves serve as instruments for characterizing the data they process. More demonstrations can be found at https://yingjiahao14.github.io/BTE-web/.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) internalize model of the linguistic world through autoregressive training at scale, yet we interact with this model almost exclusively through its final outputs, e.g., probability, generation, or judgment [4, 33]. Behind each output, however, lies sequence of internal computations: as information propagates through Transformer layers, the model progressively transforms and refines its internal state before arriving at the final prediction. Conventional evaluation observes only this endpoint, leaving the trajectory of internal change largely unused. We posit that this discarded trajectory can provide useful signal beyond the final output. On the one hand, it records how given text interacts with the linguistic and world knowledge encoded in the models parameters, potentially revealing distinctions that are obscured at the models output alone. On the other hand, it provides model-grounded view of the input: rather than relying solely on predefined human-centric properties, which may not align with the models Corresponding author. 1 own representation, we characterize an input by the predictive revisions it induces in the model. Turning this rich internal information into usable signal, however, is not trivial. First, the measurement should be principled rather than engineered: single forward pass produces large collection of high-dimensional intermediate states, admitting countless possible representations and reductions. Without principled formulation, any resulting statistic risks being an engineered feature rather than meaningful measure of the underlying trajectory of the model. Second, the signal should be useful beyond particular downstream predictor. High-dimensional internal representations can support powerful supervised classifiers, but their meaning is often tied to taskand domain-specific training. broadly useful measurement should instead carry interpretable structure on its own while remaining readily applicable across diverse tasks and domains. Third, the information should be read at the right granularity. Neuron-level analyses are fine-grained but costly and often model-specific, whereas output-level statistics collapse the computation to its endpoint. The challenge is therefore to find an intermediate representation that preserves the evolution of internal computation while remaining compact, comparable, and easy to compute. To address these challenges, we make the internal trajectory measurable through the models own predictive space. Specifically, we read each intermediate state through the models vocabulary projection as next-token predictive distribution, which we refer to as the models belief. This provides common, prediction-grounded space in which changes across layers have consistent interpretation. We then introduce Belief-Trajectory Energy (BTE) to measure these successive belief revisions. Aggregating the layerwise revisions across tokens yields compact depth profile of how the models belief evolves throughout computation. Our theoretical analysis shows that BTE is not an arbitrary measure of internal change. Locally, JensenShannon divergence induces the FisherRao geometry of the predictive distribution, giving each transition principled interpretation as an effective predictive revision. Across depth, BTE retains intermediate belief revisions that cannot be recovered from the initial-to-final change alone. Empirically, we examine whether the model-grounded information captured by BTE can serve as general measurement signal across different settings. 1) As training-free scalar, BTE consistently reflects response difficulty across diverse mathematical and reasoning tasks. Importantly, the same inputs can induce different BTE orderings under different scoring models, suggesting that BTE captures model-relative aspect of difficulty that is complementary to human-defined difficulty labels. 2) Retaining the full BTE depth profile provides richer structural information, supporting lightweight supervised readouts for humanLLM review detection and generator attribution. On paper-disjoint review detection across eight conference-years, Qwen-based BTE achieves macro-averaged AUROC of 0.998, while fine-grained BTE representations achieve 95.6% accuracy for eight-way source attribution. 3) Beyond these applications, our training analysis shows how such signals develop and change with the scoring model. BTE structure progressively emerges during pretraining and is selectively reshaped by targeted fine-tuning, demonstrating that the resulting measurement reflects what the scorer has learned and the distributions to which it has been exposed. Together, these results highlight the central perspective behind BTE: learned model can serve not only as an object of evaluation, but also as measurement instrument, providing complementary view of data through its internal predictive dynamics.

sections.title: 3 Experimental Analysis
sections.content: Here, we empirically investigate whether BTE provides useful measurement signal, proceeding from its scalar magnitude to the structure of its depth profile. First, motivated by the interpretation of BTE as effective predictive revision, we examine whether its magnitude reflects the difficulty an input poses to the scoring model in fully training-free setting, using BTE directly as scalar score (Section 3.1). Second, we examine whether the depth profile captures systematic differences in how the model processes inputs of different origins, using humanLLM review detection as testbed (Section 3.2). Finally, we ask whether these patterns are sufficiently distinctive to identify the specific model that generated an input, evaluating BTE on generator 4 attribution (Section 3.3). Unless otherwise specified, we use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [11] as the scoring model, whose homogeneous layer structure provides clean setting for analyzing belief revisions.

sections.title: 3.1 BTE as a Difficulty Indicator
sections.content: Intuitively, if BTE captures the effective predictive revisions induced during computation, inputs that are more challenging to the model may elicit stronger revisions. We therefore here study how BTE varies with difficulty across model depth, without fitting any task-specific predictor. Using BTE as scalar requires reducing its depth profile to fixed readout. Rather than averaging indiscriminately across all layers, we use the central quarter of transitions (layers 1219 for our 32-layer Llama scorer) as fixed, training-free summary. This choice is motivated by an exploratory response-disruption analysis: relative to normal responses, disrupted responses tend to exhibit lower BTE in this central window but substantially higher BTE in the final transitions (Figure 2). Because these perturbations leave the underlying problem unchanged while increasing terminal-layer BTE, high BTE near the output is not specific to problem difficulty, and averaging over the full depth may conflate qualitatively different effects. We therefore adopt the central window as conservative readout of intermediate predictive revision and test whether it tracks model-relative difficulty. We further compare central-, late-, and full-depth readouts in Appendix A.2. Figure 2 Response-disruption control. Layer-wise BTE change relative to normal responses. Experimental Setup. Using this score, we evaluate difficulty sensitivity in two settings. Within-task, inputs come from single benchmark with predefined difficulty levels, and we test whether BTE increases with difficulty. We consider MATH-500 (levels 15) [15], ProofWriter (proof depths 15) [27], StepGame (reasoning hops 15) [24], and SpaRTUN (hops 13) [21], using official reference solutions as responses. Cross-task, we compare benchmarks of increasing difficulty within the same domain: GSM8K MATH-500 OlympiadBench [14] for mathematical reasoning and StepGame SpaRTUN for spatial reasoning. By default, we score the reference solution conditioned on the problem, as solving difficulty may be expressed in the reasoning required to produce solution rather than in the problem statement alone. We use the mean BTE over the central layer set ℒ𝑀 as the scalar score 𝑒𝑀. In both settings, we report the level-wise change in 𝑒𝑀 relative to the easiest level, with 95% cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals, together with the item-level Spearman correlation 𝜌 between 𝑒𝑀 and difficulty. Because BTE provides model-grounded rather than input-intrinsic measure, we further examine the signal along two dimensions. First, we compare response BTE with problem-only BTE to determine whether difficulty is already reflected in processing the problem or becomes more apparent when processing its solution. Second, we vary the scoring model to examine how the difficulty signal depends on the model processing the input. Shown in Figure 3, we find that 1) Response BTE tracks difficulty within and across tasks. Using reference solutions as the scoring target and Llama as the scorer, 𝑒𝑀 increases consistently with difficulty on all four within-task benchmarks, with item-level Spearman correlations ranging from 𝜌 = 0.33 to 0.66 and all confidence intervals excluding zero. BTE also recovers the expected cross-task ordering for both mathematical and spatial reasoning. The cross-task result is less stable across scorers, however: three of the five scorers assign lower BTE to MATH-500 than to GSM8K. We hypothesize that this reversal may partly reflect scorer-specific training exposure that shifts the overall BTE scale of distribution. Intuitively, greater exposure to distribution during training may make its inputs more familiar to the scorer, reducing the predictive revisions they induce even when the underlying problems remain difficult. This provides possible explanation for why models with enhanced competition-level mathematical reasoning capabilities, such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B and Nemotron-Nano-8B, can invert the expected ordering between Figure 3 Level-wise change in 𝑒𝑀 relative to the easiest level, within task (top row, SpaRTUN) and across tasks (GSM8KMATH-500OlympiadBench, StepGameSpaRTUN). Solid: reference solution scored given its problem, five scorers ordered redteal by strength; dashed: problem statement only (Llama). Bars: 95% bootstrap CI (Llama). GSM8K and MATH-500. We test this hypothesis directly in Section 4. More broadly, this observation suggests potential use of BTE as probe of training exposure or model familiarity: if greater exposure systematically suppresses predictive revisions, unusually low BTE may indicate greater familiarity with given data distribution. We leave systematic investigation of this possibility to future work. 2) In contrast, problem statement need not directly reveal the computation required to solve it. This is particularly evident on ProofWriter and SpaRTUN, where difficulty is controlled by proof depth or reasoning hops while the problem statements remain largely comparable across difficulty levels. Accordingly, problem-only BTE shows little association with difficulty (𝜌 = 0.01 and 0.08), whereas response BTE exhibits substantially stronger trends (𝜌 = 0.33 and 0.66, respectively). In contrast, on MATH-500, difficulty is already reflected in the problem statement: problem-only BTE achieves 𝜌 = 0.36, compared with 𝜌 = 0.44 when scoring the reference solution. These results highlight that BTE does not define single notion of difficulty, but provides complementary model-grounded views depending on what is scored. Problem-only BTE captures difficulty expressed directly in the input but may miss computation that becomes apparent only during solving; response BTE exposes such computation but is inevitably affected by properties of the particular solution being scored. Here we explore more and detailed in Appendix A.2. 3) Difficulty sensitivity depends on the scoring model. In general, both the strongest model DeepSeek-R1Distill-Llama and the weakest model Mistral show weaker difficulty responses than intermediate-capability scorers, with mean correlations of 0.43 and 0.27, respectively, compared with 0.52 for Llama. Intuitively, model with insufficient capability may fail to differentiate inputs of varying difficulty, whereas model that is highly capable or particularly familiar with domain may exhibit less differentiated predictive revisions across the same inputs, compressing their BTE differences. This interpretation is consistent with the cross-task results above, where scorer-specific training exposure can alter the relative BTE scale across benchmarks (see Section 4 for more information). This pattern also suggests that BTE captures model-relative aspect of difficulty that is complementary to human-defined difficulty labels. The same input can induce different levels of predictive revision depending on the model processing it, making the scoring model part of the measurement itself. Practically, when using BTE to assess difficulty, the scorer should therefore be selected with respect to both its capability level and its potential training exposure to the evaluated data.

sections.title: 3.2 BTE as a Review Detector
sections.content: The preceding experiments show that even scalar summary of BTE can provide useful training-free signal for difficulty. However, collapsing BTE across depth necessarily discards where predictive revisions occur. We next ask whether the full BTE depth profile contains additional structure that can support more fine-grained distinctions about inputs. We use human-LLM review detection to test this question. Reviews typically combine synthesis of the paper with evidence-based assessments of its strengths and weaknesses, providing substantial text in which depth-wise patterns can emerge. Human and LLM reviews of the same paper share an underlying subject while having known provenance labels, reducing variation due to topic. Experimental Setup. We use real peer reviews collected and extended from ICLR and NeurIPS papers from 20212024 provided by Yu et al. [32] (detailed in Appendix A.3). For each review, we evaluate two depth profile representations: shape-only 32D, which normalizes each reviews profile across depth, and full 32D, which retains its absolute values and shape. We evaluate three training settings: (legacy-to-new transfer) trains on original human reviews and reviews from the three earlier generators on ICLR 2021 papers; the four newer generators are unseen during training. (cross-family transfer) uses the same ICLR 2021 papers but holds out one generator family at time: classifier trained on the other two families is evaluated on the held-out family, rotating among GPT, Gemini, and Claude. (full coverage) trains on papers from all eight conference-years and all seven generators, while keeping every test paper disjoint from training. We report both Original human reviews and Rewrite condition in which only the human reviews are rewritten at test time; the generated reviews and fitted classifiers remain fixed. Appendix A.3 show that this transfer is broadly consistent, although performance is relatively weaker on 2024 reviews, where the distinction between purely humanand LLM-assisted writing may itself be less clear), and remain effective even when the target generator family is entirely held out during training. The signal is also largely preserved under the Rewrite condition, suggesting that the separation is not primarily driven by superficial humanLLM stylistic cues. In particular, under cross-family transfer (Setting B), Qwen-BTE achieves macro-AUROC of 0.995, with essentially unchanged performance after rewriting (0.994). This transfer, however, does not extend uniformly across generations of LLMs. When trained only on legacy generators (Setting A), performance drops substantially on GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6, and Opus5, particularly for the Llama scorer. The depth profiles help explain this shift (Figure 4). Under both scorers, earlier generators exhibit lower BTE than human reviews across multiple depth regions. This gap progressively narrows for newer generators, particularly in the middle and final layers, and is eventually reversed by Opus-5. Notably, Qwen retains clear separation in the earlymiddle layers (AUROC 0.820.95), explaining its stronger cross-generation transfer. Importantly, this trajectory shift is accompanied by substantial increase in human-evaluated review quality. In pairwise comparisons against matched human reviews (detailed setting in Appendix A.4), GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6, and Opus-5 achieve pooled preference score of 0.878, well above human parity (0.5) and the 0.531 of the three earlier generators. Across all seven generators, human preference is strongly correlated with the signed middle-layer BTE shift relative to human reviews (𝜌 = 0.857, 𝑝 = 0.024). Thus, generators receiving higher human preference tend to exhibit BTE profiles closer to, and for Opus-5 beyond, the human distribution. These results provide possible explanation for why detection becomes harder for newer generators: improvements in human-evaluated review quality are accompanied by BTE profiles that increasingly approach the human distribution. More broadly, this shift suggests that the question may no longer be only how to distinguish model-generated reviews from human ones. As strong models produce reviews that are consistently preferred by human evaluators, their reviewing behavior may itself provide useful reference for potentially improving reviewing. 2) BTE provides strong discriminative results. With all seven generators represented in training (Setting C), Qwen-BTE reaches 0.998 macro-AUROC and Llama-BTE reaches 0.968, compared with 0.901 for Open-Anchor and below 0.868 for likelihood-based baselines. Performance remains nearly unchanged after rewriting human reviews. Open-Anchor relies on semantic similarity to reference generations and can therefore degrade when the anchor models differ substantially from the generators being detected, while likelihood-based methods reduce the models response to output-level statistics. In contrast, BTE retains both the magnitude and depth-wise structure of predictive revisions, providing richer discriminative information beyond the final predictive output. The scoring model also matters. Qwen-3.5-9B consistently outperforms Llama-3.1-8B, particularly under the cross-family and full-coverage settings. familiarity measurement points to the reason: under Qwen, the mean next-token negative log-likelihood of generated reviews is 10.4% lower than that of human reviews of the same papers, against 2.4% under Llama, and the mid-depth BTE deficit of generated reviews is correspondingly deeper (detailed in Appendix A.3). Qwen is thus substantially more familiar with model-generated text than with human text, which widens the very gap the detector exploits. plausible cause is heavier exposure to model-generated text during training, although the training mixtures are not public. Interestingly, this provides complementary view of our difficulty results (Section 3.1): scorer familiarity can reduce comparability across data distributions, but when familiarity itself differs systematically between classes, it can provide finer-grained signal for discrimination.

sections.title: 3.3 BTE for Generator Attribution
sections.content: The preceding experiments show that the BTE depth profile contains sufficient provenance information to distinguish humanfrom LLM-generated reviews. We next ask whether BTE can support finer-grained distinction: identifying which model generated review. Beyond the depth profile, we additionally retain token-level BTE patterns that are removed by token averaging, allowing us to test whether variation across both tokens and depth provides additional information for generator attribution (detailed setting in Appendix A.5). As shown in Table 2, the BTE depth profile alone already supports strong eight-way attribution, reaching 86.4% and 91.3% accuracy with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-3.5-9B, respectively. Retaining token-level variation further improves performance to 93.2% and 95.6%. The remaining errors are concentrated between GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6, which are confused with each other in roughly 10% of cases (Figure 5; more results are shown in Figure 9), while the other sources are largely well separated. These results show that generatorspecific information exists at multiple granularities of the belief trajectory, with practical trade-off between preserving finer-grained information and maintaining compact, efficient representation. sections.title: 4 Ablation Study
sections.content: Figure 5 Held-out reviews of the eight sources in the classifiers discriminant space (352D features, Llama scorer), shown with nonlinear (t-SNE) map; contours enclose 90% and 50% of each sources density, dots are centroids. Our results suggest that BTE provides model-grounded measurement whose behavior depends on the scoring model. We therefore investigate how this signal develops and changes as the model learns. We study two complementary stages of training: broad pretraining, which progressively builds the models representation of the data distribution, and targeted fine-tuning, which selectively increases exposure to particular regions of that distribution. Together, these analyses allow us to examine both how BTE emerges and how it is reshaped by what the model has learned. For the pretraining analysis, we trace OLMo-2-7B [23] across training checkpoints. For the targeted-exposure analysis, we focus on mathematical reasoning, which provides controlled difficulty labels and related data distributions with different levels of model exposure. Specifically, we fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on human-verified solutions from PRM800K [19]. Training details and additional robustness analyses are provided in Appendix A.7. 1) BTE structure emerges progressively during pretraining. We trace BTE across the pretraining process. As shown in Figure 6, the randomly initialized model exhibits virtually no input-dependent variation: the five MATH difficulty levels collapse onto the same BTE profile, with identical middle-layer means of 0.013 and 9 Figure 6 Familiarity and the depth profile. C: relative change per layer for the three training arms, with the GSM8K drop per arm shaded and the MATH-500 drop dashed as in A. As pretraining progresses, the profiles become increasingly differentiated while BTE rises overall, particularly in the middle and late layers; middle-layer BTE increases seven-fold from 0.013 to 0.093 in OLMo-2-7B [23]. In parallel, BTE becomes increasingly aligned with input difficulty: its correlation with MATH difficulty shifts from 𝜌 = 0.13 at 1T tokens to 𝜌 = +0.03 at the end of OLMo pretraining at 4T tokens, while Llama-3.1, pretrained on 15T tokens, reaches 𝜌 = +0.36. The concurrent development of BTE magnitude and difficulty sensitivity suggests that the structure captured by BTE is not simply induced by the architecture itself, but develops as the model learns the data distribution. As pretraining exposes the model to increasingly plenty of data, its predictive trajectories begin to reflect learned distinctions among inputs, which in turn become observable through BTE. 2) Fine-tuning on specific distribution systematically reduces the BTE it induces. After MATH fine-tuning, middle-layer BTE decreases by 22% on MATH-500, compared with 17% on GSM8K, eventually reversing their cross-benchmark ordering (Figure 6B). The same pattern appears within MATH: fine-tuning selectively on levels45 reduces BTE more strongly for level5 than for level 1 (19.7% vs. 17.5%). These results, aligned with the hypothesis in Section 3.1, suggest that greater targeted exposure is associated with smaller predictive revisions on the exposed distribution. Together with the pretraining results, this analysis shows that BTE reflects what the scoring model has learned: its structure develops during broad pretraining and shifts with subsequent targeted exposure. BTE therefore provides model-relative view of an input that complements properties defined independently of the scorer. Consequently, the choice and training history of the scoring model form part of the measurement itself.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: A large body of work studies the internal computation of language models through hidden states, attention patterns, neurons, and sparse features [5, 8, 9, 12, 30, 31]. Logit-lens methods provide particularly relevant perspective by projecting intermediate residual states through the models output head [3, 7, 22]. Subsequent work has used intermediate states to study knowledge recall, reasoning, and model computation. Our work shifts the objective from interpreting individual intermediate states to measuring their successive changes. More recent work has explored internal representations and activations as richer signals for estimating uncertainty [2, 5, 17], difficulty, correctness, or other properties of model inputs and outputs [29, 30]. These approaches demonstrate the value of looking beyond final predictions, but often rely on high-dimensional representations or task-specific supervised readouts. BTE instead operates directly in the models predictive distribution space and provides both training-free scalar summary and compact depth-wise representation of how predictive beliefs evolve during forward pass.

sections.title: 6 Discussion
sections.content: The central perspective behind BTE is to measure data from the models learned view of the world. Many properties of data are defined independently of the model, whereas BTE provides complementary, modelgrounded perspective by characterizing an input through the predictive revisions it induces. Consequently, BTE should not be expected to reproduce human-defined properties exactly: as our difficulty experiments illustrate, the resulting measurement can vary with both the scoring model and what is being scored. From this perspective, scorer dependence is not merely source of variation, but part of the measurement itself: different models can provide different views of the same data. More broadly, model-grounded measurement through internal model dynamics remains an emerging direction, with many open questions about how internal computation should be represented and measured. Nevertheless, the consistent patterns observed across our experiments suggest that this perspective is promising and merits further investigation.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced Belief-Trajectory Energy, model-grounded measure that characterizes an input through the predictive revisions it induces across Transformer layers. BTE provides both simple training-free signal and structured representation, showing consistent utility for difficulty measurement, humanLLM review detection, and generator attribution. Our theoretical and empirical analyses further show that BTE reflects how an input is modeled from the scorers perspective and evolves with the models training and familiarity. More broadly, our results suggest shift in perspective: learned models can serve not only as objects of evaluation, but also as measurement instruments whose internal dynamics provide complementary view of the data they process. BTE represents one step toward this direction.

Difficulty is correlated with response length (𝜌 = 0.512), and BTE itself is length-sensitive, making response length potential contributor to the observed difficulty association. We therefore compute partial Spearman correlations controlling for response length, with problem length included as an additional sensitivity analysis.
